prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "Merck & Co., Inc." (ticker MRK). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
   "nash": Tom Nash: the 12-step research process (“How to Find the Best Stocks in the Market” (Tom Nash, 2026))
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: Merck is a top dog in cancer immunotherapy through Keytruda and its shares are up about 40% in 2026, but it is a 130-year-old pharma company growing 1-3% a year with a 2028 patent cliff, not a leader of a new, fast-emerging industry. It fits few of Gardner's Rule Breaker traits beyond strong momentum and a recognisable product.
summaries.buffett: Merck has an understandable business, a long dividend record and a 74.8% gross margin, but its earnings power rests heavily on Keytruda (48.7% of 2025 sales), whose US patent expires in 2028, and recent acquisitions pushed debt to $53,906M against $7,141M of cash. At about 8.5 times book value and about 17 times charge-adjusted forward earnings, it offers little margin of safety for a business whose 10-year earnings are hard to predict.
summaries.munger: Munger would value Merck's science and the rationality of a big, cash-generating drug franchise, but inverting the problem shows clear failure paths: patent expiry, IRA price setting and PD-1/VEGF rivals such as ivonescimab. It is a decent business at a full price rather than a wonderful business at a fair one.
summaries.lynch: Merck is a classic stalwart: large, steady, dividend-paying, with sales of $65,011M growing 1.3% in 2025 and consensus about 3% for 2026. Lynch would want to buy stalwarts on dips, but after a roughly 40% rise in 2026 and a P/E far above its low growth rate, the PEG test fails.
summaries.fisher: Merck scores well on Fisher's research points, spending $15,789M on R&D in 2025 and producing Keytruda, Winrevair and the first oral PCSK9 pill Lipfendra, with a strong global sales force. Weaker points are the reliance on acquisitions to restock the pipeline and the need to replace a single product that is nearly half of sales.
summaries.graham: Merck passes Graham's size, ten-year profitability, 20-plus-year dividend and earnings-growth tests, but fails the price tests badly: about 30 times three-year average EPS and about 8.5 times book value, far above the 15x and 22.5 limits. A defensive Graham investor would not buy at today's price.
summaries.thiel: Merck holds a temporary monopoly through Keytruda's patents and a strong distribution engine, but it is not built on a 10x technology or a secret others miss, and its key monopoly ends from 2028. Durability depends on new products bought or built to replace it.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth at a reasonable price and efficient operations; Merck offers strong margins but low growth (about 3% expected for 2026) and heavy acquisition spending. It is not a beneficiary of the AI platform shift he emphasises, so it is a weak fit.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller would note the stock's strong 2026 momentum and catalysts such as the October 26 oncology investor event and Lipfendra's launch, but earnings are falling in 2026 (non-GAAP EPS guidance $2.66-$2.76 after acquisition charges) rather than accelerating. It is unlikely to be a high-conviction, concentrated bet under his approach.
summaries.smith: Merck has some Fundsmith-style traits: high gross margin, strong cash generation ($12,360M of free cash flow in 2025) and a resilient, non-cyclical industry. But returns on capital are lumpy because of large acquired R&D charges, the patent cliff threatens durability, and the price is not cheap, so it is only a partial fit.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, Merck's earnings yield is low (FY2025 operating income of about $21,218M against an enterprise value near $403B, roughly 5%) and its return on tangible capital is distorted by acquisitions. It would not rank near the top of a Magic Formula screen today.
summaries.akre: Akre's three legs are a great business, talented and honest management, and the ability to reinvest at high returns. Merck has a high-margin business and competent management, but reinvestment is mainly through costly acquisitions with uncertain returns, so the third leg is weak.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai looks for low-risk, high-uncertainty bets at deep discounts. Merck is a low-risk large business but trades well above a conservative value after a strong 2026 run, so there is no Dhandho-style mispricing.
summaries.wood: Merck is not focused on ARK's disruptive platforms such as AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing. It is an incumbent drugmaker, so it fits Cathie Wood's framework poorly.
summaries.ackman: Merck matches Ackman's preference for simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative, dominant businesses in part, with high barriers to entry. Its heavy dependence on Keytruda, the 2028 patent cliff and rising debt reduce predictability, and the price does not offer a large discount to intrinsic value.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep favoured scale-economies-shared businesses that grow stronger as they grow. Merck does not pass savings back to customers in that way, and its position in 10-20 years is less certain than today because of patent expiry, so it fits poorly.
summaries.valentine: Valentine sought huge, growing markets and a product solving a painful problem. Merck does solve painful problems such as cancer, but it is a mature incumbent rather than an early company riding a new market wave, so the fit is limited.
summaries.nash: Merck fails most of Tom Nash's 12-step screens: revenue growth is only 1-3%, debt of $53,906M exceeds cash of $7,141M, and his DCF gives about $50 per share against a $144.30 price. It passes on size, profitability over the last decade and dividend history, but scores about 55 out of 130 on his categories.

momentum.evidence: Merck shares were up about 40% year-to-date by late September 2026 with a 52-week range of $78 to $157, trading at $144.30 on October 13, 2026.

g4.evidence: Merck is run by experienced professional managers (CEO Rob Davis, research head Dean Li) and is widely held by large institutions, but it is not backed by notable star investors or visionary founders.

g6.evidence: After the 2026 rally some commentators argue the Keytruda rebuild is priced in, with the mean analyst target of about $158.64 only about 10% above the price, but most analysts still rate it a Buy.

simple.evidence: Merck sells patented medicines and vaccines, with about half of sales from one drug, Keytruda, which a careful generalist can follow, though judging drug pipelines needs some specialist knowledge.

b2.evidence: Sales rose every year from $41,518M in 2020 to $65,011M in 2025, but GAAP earnings swung sharply, from $14,519M in 2022 to $365M in 2023 and a $5,575M net loss in the first half of 2026 because of acquired R&D charges.

integrity.evidence: Merck has well-regarded governance and clear disclosure, including warning in its 10-K that US Keytruda sales will decline materially after IRA price setting, but its combined chairman-CEO role and large acquisition charges draw some criticism.

b6.evidence: Merck has bought several companies in quick succession (Verona Pharma in October 2025, Cidara and Terns Pharmaceuticals for $6.8B in 2026), much as other pharma peers facing patent cliffs have done.

roic.evidence: FY2025 net income of $18,254M was about 35% of year-end equity of $52,662M, but returns depend partly on $49,339M of debt and collapse in years with large acquired R&D charges, such as 2023 ($365M net income).

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow was $12,360M in FY2025 (about 68% of $18,254M net income) and $18,096M in FY2024, but conversion varies widely from year to year.

b10.evidence: Merck pays out much of its profit ($8,176M of dividends and $5,084M of buybacks in 2025), and retained cash spent on acquisitions such as Acceleron (Winrevair) has added value, but other deals led to multibillion-dollar write-offs and charges.

safety.evidence: A conservative DCF using Merck's 3-year average growth of 3.2% and free-cash-flow margin of 20.8% gives about $50 per share, far below the $144.30 price.

fairprice.evidence: Adding back about $5.93 per share of 2026 acquisition charges to consensus EPS of $2.68 gives about $8.61, or roughly 17 times earnings, which is about fair for a high-margin but slow-growing pharma company facing a patent cliff.

mu5.evidence: There are several clear paths to failure: Keytruda's 2028 US patent expiry, IRA price setting from 2029, PD-1/VEGF rivals such as ivonescimab, and acquisitions that fail to pay off.

reinvest.evidence: Merck reinvests heavily ($15,789M of R&D in 2025 plus large acquisitions), but returns on that spending are uncertain and lumpy, as the $9.0B Cidara and $5.7B Terns acquired R&D charges show.

ly2.evidence: Merck is a clear Lynch stalwart: a large, steady, dividend-paying drugmaker whose story is replacing Keytruda with Winrevair, Lipfendra, Keytruda Qlex and acquired drugs.

ly3.evidence: Even on charge-adjusted earnings of about $8.61 per share the P/E is about 17, far above revenue growth of about 3% and consensus long-term growth in the low single digits.

runway.evidence: Consensus sees revenue rising from $65,011M in 2025 to about $74.8B in 2028 and then flattening near $73.9B in 2030 as Keytruda loses exclusivity.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares fell from 2,547M in 2023 to 2,470M in Q2 2026 through buybacks, but no open-market insider purchases appear in the latest 90 days, while EVP Chirfi Guindo sold 10,000 shares at $135 in August 2026.

ly8.evidence: Merck is a $350B-plus company covered by about 27 analysts and widely owned by institutions.

fi2.evidence: Management is actively replacing Keytruda with new products such as subcutaneous Keytruda Qlex ($463M in Q2 2026), Winrevair ($588M in Q2 2026), Capvaxive, Enflonsia and Lipfendra.

fi3.evidence: R&D produced Keytruda, Gardasil, Capvaxive and Lipfendra, but some of the newest growth drivers (Winrevair, Ohtuvayre) came through acquisitions rather than in-house research.

fi4.evidence: Merck's global commercial reach turned Keytruda into the world's best-selling drug ($31,680M in 2025) and is driving a fast Winrevair launch, up 75% year over year in Q2 2026.

longterm.evidence: Merck spent $15,789M on R&D in 2025 and accepted large 2026 earnings charges to buy pipeline assets, showing long-term focus, while still paying a rising dividend ($0.85 per quarter in 2026).

gr1.evidence: Merck had $65,011M of sales in FY2025 and a market value of roughly $356B at $144.30 per share.

ni10.evidence: Merck reported a GAAP profit in each fiscal year from 2016 to 2025, including a small $365M in 2023, although the first half of 2026 shows a $5,575M loss from acquisition charges.

gr4.evidence: Merck has paid a quarterly dividend without interruption for decades and declared $0.85 per share for the fourth quarter of 2026.

eps10.evidence: GAAP diluted EPS rose from $1.78 (continuing operations) in FY2020 to $7.28 in FY2025, well over a one-third increase across the decade.

gr6.evidence: At $144.30 the shares trade at about 31 times the three-year average GAAP EPS of about $4.72 (FY2023 $0.14, FY2024 $6.74, FY2025 $7.28).

gr7.evidence: Price to book is about 8.5 (market value about $356B vs equity of $41,984M at June 30, 2026), and trailing P/E is above 100, so P/E times P/B is far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Keytruda is the leading PD-1 inhibitor but is not ten times better than Opdivo or Tecentriq, and ivonescimab beat it in a head-to-head lung cancer trial in China.

timing.evidence: Immuno-oncology, cardiometabolic and vaccine demand are steady, but Merck's timing is challenged by Keytruda's 2028 patent expiry and US drug-pricing reform.

th3.evidence: Merck is a century-old incumbent with sales of $65,011M, not a company expanding from dominance of a small niche.

team.evidence: CEO Rob Davis (since 2021, former CFO) and research chief Dean Li are well-regarded professional managers, but not an exceptional founder-led team.

th5.evidence: Merck has a global sales and market-access organisation reaching oncologists, vaccinators and veterinarians in many countries.

durable.evidence: Merck's scale and vaccine franchises will likely endure, but its oncology leadership is at risk after Keytruda's patents expire (US 2028, EU 2031).

th7.evidence: Merck competes in well-understood markets alongside many large rivals; its PD-1 bet was transformative but is no longer a secret.

trend.evidence: Merck benefits from ageing populations and rising cancer treatment, but it is not a leading beneficiary of platform shifts like AI or cloud computing.

dr1.evidence: Non-GAAP EPS guidance for 2026 fell to $2.66-$2.76 from $5.04-$5.16 after the Terns charge, and FY2026 consensus EPS of $2.68 is about 70% below 2025.

dr2.evidence: Over 18-24 months the one-time acquisition charges fall away and Keytruda Qlex, Winrevair and Lipfendra ramp, but the 2028 Keytruda patent cliff comes into view.

dr4.evidence: Pharma demand is insensitive to the economy, but higher interest rates raise the cost of Merck's growing $53,906M debt, and US drug-pricing policy is a headwind.

dr6.evidence: Upcoming catalysts include the October 26, 2026 oncology investor event, Q3 2026 results, the Lipfendra launch and Keytruda plus Padcev approval in Europe.

dr7.evidence: Single-product concentration in Keytruda (48.7% of 2025 sales) with a 2028 patent cliff makes Merck an unlikely candidate for a large concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin was 74.8% in FY2025 (sales $65,011M less cost of sales $16,382M).

fcfyield.evidence: FY2025 free cash flow of $12,360M is about a 3.5% yield on a market value near $356B, modest for a company growing about 3% a year.

gb2.evidence: FY2025 operating income of about $21,218M is roughly 5.3% of an enterprise value near $403B, a low earnings yield.

pa2.evidence: The 2026 earnings drop from acquisition charges and the Gardasil China slump are temporary, but the Keytruda patent cliff is a structural, not temporary, setback.

pa4.evidence: With $65,011M of diversified sales, an animal-health business and a large pipeline, a permanent loss of most of the business's value is unlikely, though the share price could fall.

wo1.evidence: Merck is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Merck's medicines are not following a steep cost-decline curve that opens up large new demand.

wo3.evidence: Merck does not combine several of ARK's innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Consensus revenue only rises to about $73.9B by 2030 from $65,011M in 2025, nowhere near many times larger.

ac3.evidence: Drug demand is largely insensitive to commodity prices and the economy, though Merck is exposed to government drug-pricing policy and some interest-rate effect on its debt.

ns1.evidence: Merck prices patented drugs for maximum value rather than passing scale savings to customers.

ns4.evidence: Merck's position in 10-20 years is less clearly strong than today because Keytruda, nearly half of sales, loses US patent protection in 2028.

va2.evidence: Keytruda treats many deadly cancers and Gardasil prevents HPV-related cancers, which are large, painful problems.

tn1.evidence: Merck is a traditional pharmaceutical company, not a business built for a secular trend like AI, energy or robotics.

tn2.evidence: The market sees Merck as a big pharma company managing a Keytruda patent cliff, which matches what it is.

tn3.evidence: Merck is a large US company, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: Revenue grew every year from 2020 to 2025 and FY2025 net income was $18,254M, passing two of three, though debt of $53,906M exceeds cash of $7,141M.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow has been positive (first-half 2026 operating cash flow $9,288M less capex $1,884M), but debt has exceeded cash in every recent quarter, e.g. $49,339M vs $14,565M at end-2025.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 1.3% in FY2025 and is expected to grow about 3% in FY2026.

tn7.evidence: FY2025 revenue growth of 1.3% plus a free-cash-flow margin of 19.0% is about 20, well below 40.

tn8.evidence: In FY2025 sales rose 1.3% while total operating costs fell from $44,256M to $43,793M, but in the latest twelve months acquired R&D charges ($22,333M of R&D in the first half of 2026) far outgrew revenue.

tn9.evidence: Merck hits instant kills: debt of $53,906M exceeds cash of $7,141M and revenue growth is below 10%, and trailing operating margin is depressed below 20% by 2026 acquisition charges.

tn10.evidence: Merck faces IRA price setting (Januvia now, Keytruda expected from 2029), most-favored-nation pricing pressure and patent litigation around Keytruda.

tn11.evidence: Merck provides patented medicines and vaccines that help patients survive cancer and prevent infections, charging health systems per dose, and doctors choose Keytruda for its broad approvals and trial evidence.

tn13.evidence: Total about 55: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 0 (TTM depressed by charges), short interest 10, institutional ownership 10, revenue vs expenses 0, 5-year return vs S&P 0, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 5, culture and mission 10, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year from 2020 to 2025 and operating margin expanded overall, but free cash flow was uneven ($9,661M in 2021, $9,143M in 2023, $12,360M in 2025) and debt exceeded cash every year.

tn15.evidence: Current ratio is 1.32 and liabilities are 2.1 times equity, but assets excluding goodwill ($108,220M) are only 1.23 times liabilities ($87,818M) at June 30, 2026, below the 2x test.

tn18.evidence: Rob Davis has grown sales from $48,704M (2021) to $65,011M (2025), but he has been CEO only since July 2021, is not a founder, and no open-market share purchases by him were found.

tn20.evidence: Merck beat Q2 2026 estimates (adjusted loss of $0.13 vs consensus $0.26 loss; sales $16.61B vs $16.33B), but a consistent multi-quarter beat record was not verified.

tn21.evidence: There is no fraud, auditor change or co-CEO structure, but Merck has made a run of acquisitions (Verona, Cidara, Terns) within about a year and an executive sold shares in August 2026 as the stock rallied.

tn22.evidence: Merck has $65,011M of revenue, strong margins, falling share count and no reliance on share sales or media hype.

tn24.evidence: At about 17 times charge-adjusted forward earnings and a 3.5% free-cash-flow yield, the price implies steady growth through a patent cliff that exceeds the roughly 1-3% revenue growth Merck is delivering.

tn25.evidence: Nash's DCF (3.2% growth, 20.8% FCF margin, 12% discount rate, 4% terminal growth, minus $46,765M net debt) gives about $50 per share, far below $144.30.

tn26.evidence: Charge-adjusted forward P/E of about 17 is in line with big-pharma peers, but with low single-digit expected earnings growth after 2026 the PEG is well above 1.
